Keeping a Paper Notebook That Lasts

Most notebooks fail in the first month, not because the paper is wrong but because the habits around it are vague. A notebook that lasts has a few plain rules. It lives in one place, it is used every day, and every page carries a date. Nothing about this is clever. The point is that a future reader, usually you, can open any page and know when it was written and what it was for. Without that, even good notes turn into a pile of fragments that nobody trusts enough to read again.

Start with the date. Write it in the top corner of every page in the same format, year first, so the pages sort the same way in your head as they do on a shelf. If a page spans two days, add the second date where the new entry starts. This costs a few seconds and saves hours later, when you are trying to remember whether a decision came before or after a meeting. Dates also make gaps visible. A week with no entries tells you something about that week, and it is better to know than to guess.

Next, keep an index. Reserve the first two pages for it and add a line whenever a page holds something you expect to look up again: a recipe, a measurement, a phone number, a plan. Number the pages by hand as you go. The index does not need to be complete. It only needs to cover the pages you will actually search for, and those are usually obvious when you write them. A notebook with an index becomes a reference instead of a diary, and a reference is the kind of thing people keep.

Paper matters less than people think, but ink matters more. Pick a pen whose ink does not fade in sunlight or smear when a page gets damp, and stick with it. Pencil is fine for sketches but rubs off over years of handling. If you tape receipts, tickets, or printed photos into the pages, use acid-free tape, because ordinary tape yellows and lifts within a few seasons. None of this needs special shopping. A plain pen and a roll of the right tape cover nearly every case.

Review is the habit most people skip. Once a week, read the pages you wrote since the last review and mark anything that needs action with a small box in the margin. Once a month, copy the open boxes forward to a fresh page so they do not get buried. Once a year, read the whole notebook from the start. That last review is slow, but it is where patterns show up: projects that kept stalling, people you meant to call, ideas that came back three times before you finally wrote them down properly.

Finally, decide where finished notebooks go. A shelf, a box, or a drawer works, as long as it is dry and the spines face out with the date range written on them. Some people scan each notebook when it fills up, which is a good backup but a poor replacement, because scans are rarely opened. The paper copy is the one you will pick up on a slow afternoon. Treat it as something worth keeping, and it will repay the small effort of dating, indexing, and reviewing every page you write.

Example Notes is a synthetic page used only in tests.
